note: Week 5 lessons: containers and Kubernetes security. Each lesson has a level (basics, intermediate or advanced) so the climb is visible.

lessons.title: Containers and Kubernetes in plain words
lessons.inOneSentence: A container packs an app with everything it needs so it runs the same anywhere, and Kubernetes is the system that runs many containers across many machines and keeps them healthy.
lessons.youCanNow: Explain the relationship between containers, Pods, nodes, namespaces and Services in Kubernetes.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Tigera, and many security companies, sell to platform engineers who run Kubernetes. You cannot design for them without their basic vocabulary: pods, nodes, namespaces and services. Today you learn it with everyday pictures, plus the cloud basics around it.
keyIdeas: You already ran a container on Day 3: Keycloak in Docker. A container is like a lunchbox: the app and everything it needs, packed so it works the same on any table.
Kubernetes is like a restaurant kitchen manager: it decides which cook (machine) prepares which dish (container), replaces a cook who goes home sick, and adds cooks when it gets busy.
A node is one machine. A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs, usually one container. A cluster is all the nodes together. A namespace is a separate area of the cluster, for example one per team.

Most clusters run in a cloud (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure). In the shared responsibility model, the cloud secures the buildings and hardware; you secure your accounts, settings, data and who can reach what.
In AWS, a VPC is your private network in the cloud, a subnet is a section of it (public if it has a route to the internet), and a security group is a firewall around a server.
Many small services talking to each other inside a cluster is called east-west traffic. Traffic coming in from users outside is north-south. Most attacks spread east-west after getting in.

words.meaning: An app packaged with everything it needs, so it runs the same anywhere.
The saved template a container is started from.
A system that runs and manages many containers across many machines.
One machine in a Kubernetes cluster.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs, usually one container.
A group of nodes managed together by Kubernetes.
A separate area inside a cluster, often one per team or app.
The cloud provider secures the infrastructure; you secure what you put on it and how you configure it.
Virtual private cloud: your own private network in a cloud provider.
Traffic between services inside a network or cluster.

steps.text: Read what a container is, and watch the short video.
Read the Kubernetes overview.
Read the first sections on pods and namespaces.
Read the shared responsibility model.
Read what a VPC is, including subnets.
Draw a picture of a small online shop running in Kubernetes: three services (web, orders, payments) in pods, on two nodes, in one namespace, inside a VPC. Mark east-west and north-south traffic.
Add the new words to your glossary with your own picture for each.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip YAML details, Helm, storage and how the Kubernetes control plane works inside.
checkYourself: Explain containers and Kubernetes with the lunchbox and kitchen pictures.
What is the difference between a pod, a node and a cluster?
In the shared responsibility model, give two things that stay your responsibility.
lookFor: A container packs an app with everything it needs, like a lunchbox that works on any table. Kubernetes is the kitchen manager that decides where each dish is cooked, replaces cooks who leave and adds cooks when busy.
A pod is the smallest unit that runs (usually one container), a node is a machine that runs pods, and a cluster is all the nodes managed together.
For example: who has access to your cloud accounts, how your network and security groups are configured, and protecting your data. The provider secures the data centres and hardware.

lessons.title: Kubernetes networking and network policy
lessons.inOneSentence: By default every pod in a Kubernetes cluster can talk to every other pod; network policies are the rules that limit this, and tools like Calico enforce them.
lessons.youCanNow: Explain how a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy selects Pods by label, and state that enforcement requires a supporting network plugin such as Calico.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is the problem Tigera exists to solve, and the heart of case study 2. Platform engineers know default-allow is risky, but switching to default-deny can break apps. Designers help them see traffic, write policies safely and roll them out with confidence.
keyIdeas: From Week 3 you know access rules for people and devices. Network policy is the same idea for services inside a cluster.
Kubernetes finds things by labels, like name tags: app=orders, team=payments. A network policy picks pods by label, not by name or address, because pods come and go.
A Service gives a group of pods one stable name and address, so web can always reach “orders” even as pods restart.

Default allow: in a namespace with no NetworkPolicy selecting a pod, everything can reach it. This default-allow behaviour, and NetworkPolicy enforcement itself, both depend on the cluster running a network plugin (CNI) that supports NetworkPolicy, such as Calico — without one, a NetworkPolicy you write is simply not enforced, even though Kubernetes accepted it.

A network policy says, for example: “pods labelled app=payments-db accept traffic only from pods labelled app=payments on port 5432.” Once a pod is selected by any policy, everything else to it is denied.
Calico (open source, by Tigera) enforces network policies and adds its own features. Cloud security groups are stateful: if a request is allowed in, its reply is allowed out automatically.
Mutual TLS (mTLS) is TLS where both sides prove who they are, not only the server. Service meshes use it so each service knows exactly which service is calling.

words.meaning: A key-value tag on a Kubernetes object, such as app=orders.
A rule that picks objects by their labels.
A stable name and address for a group of pods.
A Kubernetes rule that limits which pods can talk to which.
Traffic coming in to a pod, and traffic going out of it.
Tigera’s open-source networking and network security for Kubernetes.
A firewall that remembers allowed connections and lets their replies through.
Mutual TLS: both sides of a connection prove who they are.
A layer that manages and secures traffic between services, often with mTLS.

steps.text: Read about labels and selectors.
Read the introduction and first example of Services.
Read Network Policies up to and including the default policies.
Read About Calico.
Read about security groups and notice the word “stateful”.
Read what mutual TLS is.
Add labels to your Day 29 shop picture and write two network policies for it in plain words, then in the shape of a policy (selector, from, ports).

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip CNI internals, eBPF and service mesh setup. Understand labels, default allow and what a policy says.
checkYourself: Why does Kubernetes use labels rather than pod names in network policies?
What does “default allow” mean, and why is it risky?
How does mTLS differ from ordinary TLS?
lookFor: Pods are created and destroyed all the time and get new names and addresses. Labels describe what a pod is (app=orders), so a policy keeps working as pods change.
With no policies, every pod can reach every other pod. If one service is compromised, the attacker can move freely to databases and other services.
In ordinary TLS only the server proves who it is. In mTLS both sides do, so the server also knows exactly which client or service is calling.

lessons.title: Exercise 11: a local cluster with Calico
lessons.inOneSentence: You will run a small Kubernetes cluster on your laptop with Calico and deploy a demo app, so pods, services and namespaces become real things you can see.
lessons.youCanNow: Set up a local Kubernetes cluster with Calico and apply a basic network policy.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Platform engineers live in terminals and YAML. Doing their setup once, slowly and with notes, gives you empathy for their work and a true sense of what is hard, which you will need for case study 2 interviews.
keyIdeas: kind runs a whole Kubernetes cluster inside Docker on your laptop. It is free and you can delete it at any time.
kubectl is the command-line tool for talking to the cluster: kubectl get pods shows what is running.
Calico installs as pods in the cluster itself and then controls networking for all other pods.
A demo app with three or four small services is enough. Many Kubernetes tutorials have one; any simple web plus backend works.
Take notes as a designer: where you waited, what failed, which error messages helped and which did not.

words.meaning: Kubernetes in Docker: a tool for running a cluster on your laptop.
The command-line tool for controlling a Kubernetes cluster.
A text format used to describe Kubernetes objects.
To start an app on a cluster.
Container network interface: the plug-in that gives pods networking, here Calico.

steps.text: Install kind and create a cluster, following the quick start.
Install Calico on kind, following the guide step by step.
Deploy a small demo app with at least two services in its own namespace. Check it with kubectl get pods and get services.
Draw your real cluster: namespaces, pods, labels and services, using kubectl output.
Write designer notes: three moments of confusion and one thing a visual tool could have shown you.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip cloud clusters, Helm charts and Calico Enterprise features. A local cluster with a small app is the goal.
checkYourself: What do kind, kubectl and Calico each do in your setup?
What would a platform engineer need from a visual tool that the terminal did not give you?
lookFor: kind runs the cluster in Docker on your laptop, kubectl lets you control and inspect it, and Calico provides pod networking and enforces network policies.
For example: a map of which services talk to which, the labels on each pod, and a clear view of what is allowed or blocked, without running many commands.

lessons.title: Exercise 12: break and fix a network policy
lessons.inOneSentence: You will turn on default deny, watch your app break, then write policies to fix it, noting exactly how you found the cause.
lessons.youCanNow: Change a network policy, observe the resulting connectivity break, and explain why it happened.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: This is the core pain of case study 2: default deny is safe but scary, because a missing rule silently breaks an app. Living through it once gives you the evidence and empathy to design a better way.
keyIdeas: A default-deny policy selects every pod in a namespace and allows nothing. After applying it, your app will stop working. That is the point.
Breakage is often silent: requests time out, with no message that says “blocked by policy”. Finding the cause takes time and experience.
Fix it one connection at a time: web to orders, orders to the database, and DNS (pods must still reach the cluster’s DNS service, a common forgotten rule).
Test after each policy: does the app work, and is anything still allowed that should not be?
Write down how you found each cause. Your debugging path is research data for a tool that could make it faster.

words.meaning: A policy that blocks all traffic not explicitly allowed.
When a request waits for a reply that never comes.
A policy rule that lets specific traffic through.
Finding and fixing the cause of a problem.

steps.text: Read about default deny before you apply it.
Work through the Kubernetes network policy examples in your cluster.
Apply default deny to your app’s namespace. Record what breaks and what you see.
Fix it policy by policy, including DNS. Test after each one.
Write it up: what broke, how you found each cause, how long it took, and what a tool could show to make it faster.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Skip Calico’s global and tiered policies unless you finish early; the optional reference covers them.
checkYourself: Why is default deny both safe and scary?
What rule is commonly forgotten after default deny, and why?
How did you find the cause of each break, and what would have made it faster?
lookFor: Safe because nothing can talk unless allowed, so an attacker cannot move freely. Scary because any missing rule breaks the app, often with no clear message.
Allowing DNS. Pods need to look up service names through the cluster’s DNS, so without that rule almost everything fails, even with the right app rules.

A good answer describes the real path (for example checking pods, guessing, reading logs, testing with a tool) and proposes something concrete, such as showing denied connections next to the policy that blocked them.

lessons.title: Case study 2 kickoff: why network policies are hard
lessons.inOneSentence: You will start your second case study by researching why platform engineers find network policies hard, and how Tigera and its competitors try to help.
lessons.youCanNow: Research why network-policy work is hard for platform teams and identify a specific user and problem.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: Case study 2 should show you can design for a highly technical user and a core problem of a company like Tigera. Today’s research grounds it: competitor patterns, public evidence and your own Exercise 12 notes.
keyIdeas: Your working question: “How might we help platform engineers move from default allow to least-privilege network policy without breaking their apps?”
One pattern is policy recommendations: watch real traffic for a while, then suggest policies that allow only what was seen. Calico Cloud does this.
Another is staged policies: apply a policy in “would block” mode first, see what it would have blocked, then enforce it.
A third is visual traffic maps: Cilium’s Hubble and Calico’s tools show which services talk, so engineers can see before they write.
Evidence to collect: forum and GitHub issues, conference talks and blog posts about network policy pain, and one conversation with a platform engineer.

words.meaning: A suggested policy generated from observed traffic.
A policy that reports what it would block without blocking yet.
A picture of which services talk to which.
Each service may reach only what it truly needs.
An engineer who builds and runs the infrastructure other teams deploy on.

steps.text: Read Calico’s policy recommendations page closely and screenshot the key ideas.
Read about staged policies: preview impact, then enforce.
Look at Cilium Hubble’s observability screenshots for comparison.
Collect at least eight pieces of public evidence about network policy pain (GitHub issues, forums, talks) in your research log.
Arrange a 20-minute chat with one platform or DevOps engineer, and write five questions.
Write your three strongest observations so far, each with evidence, including your Exercise 12 notes.

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not design screens yet. Compare patterns and collect evidence.
checkYourself: What is your case study 2 question?
Explain policy recommendations and staged policies in one sentence each.
lookFor: For example: “How might we help platform engineers move from default allow to least-privilege network policy without breaking their apps?” It names the user, the move and the fear.
Recommendations: the tool watches real traffic and suggests policies that allow only what it saw. Staged policies: you apply a policy in a “would block” mode first, see its effect, then enforce it.

lessons.title: Case study 2 problem statement: write it up and share
lessons.inOneSentence: You will write the case study 2 problem statement and the journey of a platform engineer securing a cluster.
lessons.youCanNow: Define the user and problem statement for a network-policy product.
lessons.whyItMattersToADesigner: A clear journey shows where the fear and the risk are, which is where your design will act. Sharing it early with engineers keeps your technical understanding honest.
keyIdeas: The journey: discover what talks to what, write a first policy, test it, roll it out, and keep it right as apps change. Mark the emotions: confident, unsure, afraid.
Users: the platform engineer (writes and owns policies), app developers (their apps might break) and the security team (wants least privilege and proof).
Evidence comes from your Exercise 12 debugging, public posts and your conversations.
Success metrics might be: share of namespaces with policies, time from observed traffic to enforced policy, and incidents caused by policy changes.
You have moved from containers basics to a real product problem in one week. Notice that progression in how you write: use the right terms, but explain them.

words.meaning: A picture of the steps a user takes, with their thoughts and feelings.
How much of a cluster is protected by policies.
Putting a change into effect, often in stages.
Someone affected by or responsible for an outcome.

steps.text: Read journey mapping 101.
Draw the platform engineer’s journey with steps, thoughts, feelings and risky moments.
Write the problem statement (300–500 words): users, problem, evidence, impact, constraints and success metrics.
Share it with one engineer or post a short version, and note the reply.
Compare it with your case study 1 problem statement: what is similar, what is different?

lessons.skipOrSkim: Do not decide the solution yet. Keep the statement neutral.
checkYourself: Who are the three people affected by network policy in a company?
Write one success metric for case study 2.
lookFor: The platform engineer who writes and owns the policies, the app developers whose services could break, and the security team who needs least privilege and proof of it.
For example: time from observed traffic to an enforced policy, the share of namespaces protected by policy, or the number of incidents caused by policy changes.
